title: Can good management keep primary health centers open in crises?
gist: World Bank research using an adapted World Management Survey of 429 Kenyan primary health centers finds very low management scores (1.61 vs US 3.11); during COVID-19 and the 2020-21 health workers' strike, private PHCs held up better, and among private PHCs a 1 SD higher management score was associated with 6.5 p.p. higher outpatient attendance, driven by operational practices, while management did not help public PHCs lacking autonomy.

themes.theme: Measuring management in Kenyan primary care

insights.claim: An adapted World Management Survey covered 429 primary health centers and 73 hospitals across Kenya in 2021, linked to monthly outpatient data from Kenya's Health Management Information System.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Novel facility-level evidence base for health-system performance in Africa.

insights.claim: Kenya's primary health centers averaged a management score of just 1.61 on a 1-5 scale, below India (1.87), Brazil (2.20) and the United States (3.11), with most clustered near the bottom.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Large management-quality gap suggests big productivity upside from operational upgrades.
insights.quote: Kenya's PHCs averaged a management score of just 1.61
insights.locator: PHC’s adoption of structured management practices

themes.theme: Resilience during COVID-19 and the strike

insights.claim: Both public and private Kenyan PHCs saw attendance declines in the first COVID-19 year, but during the December 2020-January 2021 public health workers' strike public PHC attendance fell while private PHCs stayed comparatively stable, consistent with patients shifting to private providers.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Private providers capture demand when public systems are disrupted, relevant for private healthcare operators in mixed systems.
insights.quote: public PHC attendance fell while private PHCs remained comparatively stable

insights.claim: Within private PHCs, a one standard deviation higher management score was associated with 6.5 percentage points higher outpatient attendance during disruptions relative to before.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Management quality is a measurable resilience factor for private clinic chains.
insights.quote: A one standard deviation increase in management score was associated with 6.5 percentage points higher outpatient attendance

insights.claim: Operational practices such as managing patient flow, tracking supplies, following protocols and using data to spot problems mattered most, while people-management practices like hiring and incentives were less strongly associated with crisis attendance.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Operational systems, not HR practices, drive service continuity under shocks.

insights.claim: In public PHCs better management did not translate into maintained services, suggesting management practices are less useful when managers lack autonomy, tools or resources.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Public health reform needs decentralization of authority, not just training.

themes.theme: Policy lessons for mixed health systems

insights.claim: Operations management in essential service delivery is not a 'soft' issue and can determine whether a PHC continues to deliver services in a crisis.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Investment in clinic operations systems has resilience payoffs.

insights.claim: Mixed health systems should account for the complementary role private facilities already play during disruptions and regulate and integrate that role more deliberately.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Supports public-private integration policies benefiting private primary-care providers.
insights.quote: health planners can no longer afford to treat the two sectors as unrelated
